Potential Difference, commonly called voltage. The work done per unit charge by an electric field in moving a charge between two points, expressed in volts and quantifying the driving force for electron movement in a circuit.

Potential difference is defined as the difference in electric potential energy between two points divided by the charge. One volt equals one joule per coulomb, representing the energy transferred per unit charge. In a circuit, potential difference drives current flow. Higher voltage creates a stronger electrical force on charge carriers, analogous to how higher pressure difference drives fluid faster. A circuit element maintains a potential difference across itself equal to the product of current and resistance—this is Ohm's Law, expressed as voltage equals current times resistance. The voltage drop across the element follows this relationship. Battery voltage is the maximum potential difference they can sustain. A nine-volt battery maintains a nine-volt potential difference between its terminals when supplying current. Ground is arbitrarily chosen as the reference point of zero potential. All other voltages in a circuit are measured relative to ground, though only potential difference has physical meaning. Potential difference determines the energy delivered to a circuit. Power equals voltage times current, so higher voltage enables more power delivery through the same conductor. Potential difference arises directly from the electric field, the fundamental phenomenon underlying it and created by charge distribution, and drives the flow of current in a conductor.
